English abstract Context: Well-functioning fishway passes are needed worldwide to promote fish migration as the number of barriers is unlikely to decrease in the future. The Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) was designed to provide a simple, compact solution for fish to overcome barriers between 1 m and 10 m high. It features a multi-chamber valve system with adjustable current options in both the inflow and outflow chambers. The principle is as follows: fish are attracted by the flow at the lower valve when it starts to open, enter the system when the lower valve fully opens and make their way towards the upper valve, to then exit when the upper valve opens. Aim: Before new designs of fishway passes are introduced, there should be some rigorous testing of the attraction, entrance, passage and overall efficiency. The aim of this report was to assess how well the FSSG functions under experimental conditions and to understand how fish behave before, during and after passage. Methods: Testing consisted of three experiments with ide (Leuciscus idus). Pit tags were inserted in fish, which allowed to determine when tagged fish passed the lower valve and upper valve as both were equipped with antennas. In addition, the opening and closing of the valves were monitored. The obtained data allowed to determine the different types of fishway efficiency, the time of entrance and passage, the moment of entrance and exit in function of the valve openings, and the effect of length, weight and species on aforementioned aspects. Results: Despite operational settings of the FSSG throughout the experiments being fixed, entrance efficiency and passage efficiency varied substantially as they ranged from 70 % to 98 %, and from 68 % to 84 %, respectively. Entrance time (time from release to entry) and passage time (time from entry to exit) were relatively high. 50% of all tagged fish had an entrance time of 100 to 200 minutes, while the entered fish had a passage time of 225 to 1200 minutes. The length and weight did not seem to have any effect on whether fish were able to successfully use the fish spiral, nor did it have an effect on the time it took fish to move up the fish spiral. Fish generally wait until the valves are completely open before entering and leaving the FSSG, though for the upper valve a relatively large amount of fish also seem to leave the FSSG when the valve is opening or closing. Some preliminary tests with other species indicated there was no clear difference between species in the passage succes or passage timing. Implications: Under the experimental conditions tested, entrance and passage efficiencies were relatively high and within the range reported for several other fishway types. Direct comparison with field-tested fishways should, however, be interpreted cautiously because of major differences in experimental conditions. The high variability of both efficiencies is also in line with findings in literature of other fishway designs and highlights the strong effect local conditions and placement could have. However, it should be noted that the calculated entrance and passage efficiency are most likely to be overestimated and underestimated, respectively, from the actual efficiencies that were obtained in this lab setting. It was unfortunately not possible to quantify these levels of uncertainty. Therefore field testing under representative conditions is needed to assess how the FSSG performs in real-life situations. In addition, attraction efficiency could not be tested in this set-up, but might be an important aspect to consider, especially given its strong link with local conditions and placement. As attraction flow can be adapted in the FSSG, it will be important to test out different settings per site. The relatively long transit times were to be expected because the FSSG works in phases and the speed with which a fish can travel is therefore not only determined by its own traits and motivation, but also by the operational settings of the FSSG. Conclusion: The experiments on the FSSG yielded promising results. However, it should be stressed that the fixed laboratory settings of this study prevented the assessment of the attraction efficiency, a key aspect in fishway design that often turns out to be the limiting factor, and also introduced some serious uncertainty regarding the entrance (overestimation) and passage efficiency (underestimation). Any extrapolation to the wide range of real-life situations should therefore be done with care. Well-advised placement, scientifically sound follow-up and consequent adjustments are key to get the most out of the potential of the FSSG.

Nederlandstalige samenvatting Context: Goed functionerende vispassages zijn cruciaal om vismigratie te bevorderen, aangezien het aantal barrières in de toekomst waarschijnlijk niet zal afnemen. De Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) werd ontworpen om een eenvoudige, compacte oplossing te bieden voor vissen om barrières tussen 1 m en 10 m hoog te overwinnen. De FFSG bestaat uit een verticale Archimedesschroef met drie “kanalen” die alle drie onderaan en bovenaan een afsluitbare schuif hebben met instelbare openingsopties, en die zowel bovenaan als onderaan uitkomen in 1 instroom- en 1 uitstroomcompartiment. Het principe is als volgt: vissen worden aangetrokken door de stroming bij de onderste klep wanneer deze begint te openen, komen in het systeem wanneer de onderste klep volledig opent en banen zich een weg naar de bovenste klep, om er vervolgens weer uit te zwemmen wanneer de bovenste klep opent. Doel: Voordat nieuwe concepten van vispassages worden geïntroduceerd, moeten de attractie-efficiëntie, de ingangsefficiëntie, de passage-efficiëntie en de algehele efficiëntie grondig worden getest. Het doel van dit rapport was om te beoordelen hoe goed de FSSG functioneert onder experimentele omstandigheden en om te begrijpen hoe vissen zich gedragen voor, tijdens en na de passage. Methoden: Tests bestonden uit drie experimenten met winde (Leuciscus idus). Er werden pit-tags ingebracht in de vissen, waardoor bepaald kon worden wanneer de gemerkte vissen de onderste klep en de bovenste klep passeerden, aangezien beide waren uitgerust met antennes. Bovendien werd het openen en sluiten van de schuiven opgevolgd. De verkregen data maakten het mogelijk om de verschillende types van efficiëntie van de FSSG te bepalen, het tijdstip van binnenkomen en passeren, het moment van binnenkomen en verlaten in functie van de klepopeningen, en het effect van lengte, gewicht en soort op voornoemde aspecten. Resultaten: Ondanks het feit dat de operationele instellingen van de FSSG tijdens de experimenten vast stonden, varieerden de ingangsefficiëntie en de passage-efficiëntie aanzienlijk, respectievelijk van 0,70 tot 0,98 en van 0,68 tot 0,84. De ingangstijd (tijd van loslaten tot binnenkomen) en de passagetijd (tijd van binnenkomen tot verlaten) waren relatief hoog. 50% van alle gemerkte vissen had een ingangstijd van 100 tot 200 minuten, terwijl de binnengekomen vissen een passagetijd hadden van 225 tot 1200 minuten. De lengte en het gewicht leken geen effect te hebben op de vraag of vissen in staat waren om met succes gebruik te maken van de FSSG, noch op de tijd die vissen nodig hadden om zich omhoog te bewegen in de FSSG. Vissen wachten over het algemeen tot de schuiven helemaal open zijn voordat ze de FSSG binnengaan en verlaten, hoewel voor de bovenste klep ook relatief veel vissen de FSSG lijken te verlaten wanneer de klep open of dicht gaat. Uit enkele preliminaire testen met andere soorten bleek dat er geen duidelijk verschil was tussen de soorten wat betreft het succes of de timing van de passage. Implicaties: Onder de geteste experimentele condities, waren de ingangs- en passage-efficiëntie relatief hoog en vielen binnen de gerapporteerde waarden van andere vispassage-types. De hoge variabiliteit van beide efficiënties komt ook overeen met bevindingen in de literatuur over andere ontwerpen en benadrukt het sterke effect dat lokale omstandigheden en plaatsing kunnen hebben. Er moet wel opgemerkt te worden dat de berekende ingangs- en passage-efficiëntie hoogstwaarschijnlijk respectievelijk overschat en onderschat worden t.o.v. de echte waarden die bereikt werden in dit experiment. Het was helaas niet mogelijk om de onzekerheidsniveaus van deze metrices te kwantificeren. Daarom zijn veldtesten onder representatieve condities nodig om na te gaan hoe de FSSG werkt in echte situaties. Daarnaast kon de attractie-efficiëntie niet worden getest in deze opstelling, maar dit zou een belangrijk aspect kunnen zijn om rekening mee te houden, vooral gezien het sterke verband met lokale omstandigheden en plaatsing. Aangezien de attractiestroom in de FSSG kan worden aangepast, is het belangrijk om verschillende instellingen per locatie te testen. De relatief lange doorlooptijden waren te verwachten omdat de FSSG gefaseerd werkt en de snelheid waarmee een vis zich kan verplaatsen dus niet alleen bepaald wordt door zijn eigen toestand en motivatie, maar ook door de operationele instellingen van de FSSG. Conclusie: De experimenten met de FSSG leverden veelbelovende resultaten op. Er moet echter benadrukt worden dat de vaste laboratoriumopstelling van deze studie het onmogelijk maakte om de attractie-efficiëntie te beoordelen, een sleutelaspect in het ontwerp van vismigratievoorzieningen dat vaak de beperkende factor blijkt te zijn, en dat er ook ernstige onzekerheid bestond over de inschattingen van de ingangsefficiëntie (overschatting) en de passage-efficiëntie (onderschatting). Elke extrapolatie naar de brede waaier van reële situaties moet daarom voorzichtig gebeuren. Een weloverwogen plaatsing, wetenschappelijk verantwoorde opvolging en consequente bijsturing zijn essentieel om het potentieel van de FSSG optimaal te benutten.

Résumé français Contexte: Des passes à poissons performantes sont absolument nécessaires pour favoriser la migration des poissons, car il est peu probable que le nombre d’obstacles diminue à l’avenir. Le Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) a été conçu pour fournir une solution simple et compacte permettant aux poissons de franchir des obstacles d’une hauteur comprise entre 1 et 10 m. Il est doté d’un système de vannes à plusieurs chambres avec des options de courant réglables à l’entrée comme à la sortie. Elle est dotée d’un système de vannes à chambres multiples avec des options de courant réglables dans les chambres d’entrée et de sortie. Le principe est le suivant : les poissons sont attirés par le courant au niveau de la vanne inférieure lorsqu’elle commence à s’ouvrir, entrent dans le système lorsque la vanne inférieure s’ouvre complètement et se dirigent vers la vanne supérieure, pour ensuite sortir lorsque la vanne supérieure s’ouvre. Objectif: Avant d’introduire de nouveaux modèles de passes à poissons, il convient de tester rigoureusement l’attraction, l’entrée, le passage et l’efficacité globale. L’objectif de ce rapport était d’évaluer le fonctionnement de la FSSG dans des conditions expérimentales et de comprendre le comportement des poissons avant, pendant et après le passage. Méthodes: Les essais ont consisté en trois expériences avec l’ide (Leuciscus idus). Des marques de fosse ont été insérées dans les poissons, ce qui a permis de déterminer quand les poissons marqués passaient la vanne inférieure et la vanne supérieure, toutes deux étant équipées d’antennes. En outre, l’ouverture et la fermeture des valves ont été surveillées. Les données obtenues ont permis de déterminer les différents types d’efficacité des passes à poissons, le temps d’entrée et de passage, le moment de l’entrée et de la sortie en fonction de l’ouverture des vannes, et l’effet de la longueur, du poids et de l’espèce sur les aspects susmentionnés. Résultats: Bien que les paramètres opérationnels du FSSG aient été fixes tout au long des expériences, l’efficacité d’entrée et l’efficacité de passage ont varié de manière substantielle, allant respectivement de 0,70 à 0,98 et de 0,68 à 0,84. Le temps d’entrée (temps écoulé entre la libération et l’entrée) et le temps de passage (temps écoulé entre l’entrée et la sortie) étaient relativement élevés. 50 % de tous les poissons marqués avaient un temps d’entrée de 100 à 200 minutes, tandis que les poissons entrés avaient un temps de passage de 225 à 1 200 minutes. La longueur et le poids ne semblent pas avoir d’effet sur la capacité des poissons à utiliser avec succès la spirale à poissons, ni sur le temps qu’il faut aux poissons pour remonter la spirale à poissons. Les poissons attendent généralement que les vannes soient complètement ouvertes avant d’entrer dans le FSSG et d’en sortir, bien que pour la vanne supérieure, un nombre relativement important de poissons semble également quitter le FSSG lorsque la vanne s’ouvre ou se ferme. Des tests préliminaires menés avec d’autres espèces ont indiqué qu’il n’y avait pas de différence significative entre les espèces en termes de taux de réussite ou de durée de passage. Implications: Dans les conditions expérimentales testées, les efficacités d’entrée et de passage étaient relativement élevées et se situaient dans la fourchette rapportée pour plusieurs autres types de passes à poissons. Une comparaison directe avec des passes à poissons testées sur le terrain doit toutefois être interprétée avec prudence en raison de différences majeures dans les conditions expérimentales. La forte variabilité de ces deux efficacités est également conforme aux résultats de la littérature concernant d’autres conceptions de passes à poissons et souligne l’impact majeur que peuvent avoir les conditions locales et l’emplacement. Cependant, il convient de noter que les efficacités d’entrée et de passage calculées sont très probablement respectivement surestimées et sous-estimées par rapport aux efficacités réelles obtenues dans ce cadre de laboratoire. Il n’a malheureusement pas été possible de quantifier ces niveaux d’incertitude ; par conséquent, des essais sur le terrain dans des conditions représentatives sont nécessaires pour évaluer le comportement du FSSG en situation réelle. De plus, l’efficacité d’attraction n’a pas pu être testée dans ce dispositif, mais elle pourrait constituer un aspect important à prendre en compte, notamment en raison de son lien étroit avec les conditions locales et l’emplacement. Le débit d’attraction pouvant être adapté dans le FSSG, il sera important de tester différents réglages selon les sites. Les temps de transit relativement longs étaient prévisibles car le FSSG fonctionne par phases ; la vitesse à laquelle un poisson peut se déplacer n’est donc pas seulement déterminée par ses propres caractéristiques et sa motivation, mais aussi par les réglages opérationnels du FSSG. Conclusion: Les expériences sur le FSSG ont donné des résultats prometteurs. Toutefois, il convient de souligner que les conditions de laboratoire fixes de cette étude ont empêché l’évaluation de l’efficacité de l’attraction, un aspect clé de la conception des passes à poissons qui s’avère souvent être le facteur limitant, et ont également introduit une sérieuse incertitude concernant l’efficacité de l’entrée (surestimation) et du passage (sous-estimation). Toute extrapolation à la vaste gamme de situations réelles doit donc être effectuée avec précaution. Un placement judicieux, un suivi scientifiquement fondé et des ajustements conséquents sont essentiels pour tirer le meilleur parti du potentiel du FSSG.

1 Introduction 1.1 Context Migration barriers and habitat fragmentation are the main threats impacting freshwater and diadromous fish species globally (Belletti et al., 2020). Though barrier removal is often the preferred course of action, it is not always feasible because of economical or safety-related reasons. Potential other solutions to promote fish movement include fish passes and fish elevators, though there efficiency is often strongly dependent on the local conditions and target species (Noonan et al., 2012). Therefore these systems need to be thoroughly assessed to understand how the efficiency is determined by the environmental conditions and target species. 1.2 Design of the Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) The Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) of Vandezande was designed to provide a simple, compact solution for fish to overcome barriers between 1 m and 10 m high. It consists of three winded immobile “canals” shaped as a vertical Archimedes’ screw, each with an entry (i.e., the lower valves) and exit (i.e., the upper valves). The lower and upper valves are surrounded by an outflow/inflow chamber. Each canal has an artificial substratum from gravel that is glued on the Archimedes’ screw, is completely filled with water and contains five pressure sensors: three throughout the canal, one at the entrance and one at the exit. The lower and upper valves are adjusted accordingly to the pressure inside of the canal. When the lower valve is fully opened then the upper valve opening is at its smallest. The main idea is for fish to be attracted by the flow at the lower valve when it starts to open, enter the system when the lower valve fully opens and make their way towards the upper valve, to then exit the “canal” when the upper valve opens. 1.3 Aims The aim of this study is to assess the efficiency of the FSSG and understand how fish of different species and sizes respond to its mechanisms. In doing so, recommendations can be formulated on how appropriate and feasible the use of the FSSG for fish passage would be under different conditions. The assessment was done via an experimental set-up under controlled conditions with live fish. 1.4 Experimental set-up As the FSSG is a relatively complex system, designed to enable safe passage via the subsequent opening of multiple valves, a traditional set-up in which fish are provided at the entrance and recaptured at the exit to determine mortality rate and type of injuries, would be insufficient (Bierschenk et al., 2018). To really understand the system and how it affects migrating fish, there are more questions to be answered than the general question: How many fish make it through the exit? More specifically, questions that need to be answered are: When do fish enter the FSSG, when do they leave it, how much time (or cycles) does it take them to find the entrance and move up the FSSG, how does experience with the system alter fish behaviour and how does the fish size and species determine the passage efficiency? The unique operating conditions of the FSSG and multiple questions to be answered, required an alternative assessment approach. In 2023 preliminary tests were conducted to test different methodologies. Fyke net experiments and pit telemetry experiments were evaluated and fine-tuned to come up with a sound methodology that was used during multiple experiments of 2024. The fyke net experiments, which involved fish release and recapture, were found insufficient to provide sound insights as only few fish could be recaptured. For this reason, in 2024, fyke nets were replaced with a recapture method that utilises dip nets, offering the fish more space and shelter in the upper basin and inflow compartment. In 2023 multiple fish species were used during the preliminary tests, but to provide enough statistical power to draw sound conclusions it was decided to use one species instead for which sufficient individuals were used. The aim of this set-up was to encourage fish to remain in the upper basin until the end of each experiment. The PIT telemetry experiments on the other hand were found to be very suitable in combination with the new recapture method and after some tests to optimize placement and detection probability, the methodology was fixed. 1.5 PIT (Passive Integrated Transponder) telemetry PIT telemetry is a widely used technology, enabling the tracking of fish or terrestrial animals, especially in narrow systems (Thorstad et al., 2013). Similar to other telemetry techniques, it relies on a tag inserted or fixed on a fish but also on an antenna, which generates a magnetic field, charging the tag which then emits a response that can be read by the system (Bubb et al., 2002). Two types of PIT telemetry exist: Half-Duplex (HDX) and Full-Duplex (FDX). In FDX systems, the antenna continuously generates a magnetic field and the tag response can constantly be detected and recorded. HDX systems switch between the “generating a magnetic field” mode and “reading tag response” mode. Antennae are simpler in HDX, can be larger and also require less power. They are usually made from single or multiple loops of insulated wired electrical cable, generating the magnetic field. This antenna is then connected to a tuning box, which is linked to a reader box where the data logging computer is located (Barbour et al., 2011). The tracked animal is usually tagged internally in the abdominal cavity with a different tag depending on whether the system is HDX or FDX. Tags of different sizes can be used, with the large ones having a strong signal and the smaller ones having a weaker signal. The signal range can be impacted by the presence of metal around the antennae, although it is often still usable. HDX telemetry was used in the present study. 2 Methods 2.1 Description of the FSSG 2.2 Set-up 2.3 Fish experiments 2.4 Data processing

2 Methods 2.1 Description of the FSSG The FSSG or Fish Spiral Sluice Gate or ‘Fischwendelschleuse’ is a fish passage with an adjustable attracting current aimed for all fish species (Fig. 2.1). This system enables continuous sluice operation and should also accommodate bottom-dwelling fish. It features an individually doped multi-chamber lock system with adjustable current options in both the inflow and outflow chambers. Figuur 2.1: Operating principle of the FSSG. The fish pass is designed to be as natural as possible via a natural substrate base and upright built (i.e., not rotating) (Fig. 2.2). The lock control is adaptable for each lock chamber to suit different target fish species. The FSSG lock is compact, suitable for fall heights of 1 to 10 meters. It has few moving parts and simple controls. Currently, the FSSG lock is being designed with diameters of 2 to 5 meters and flow rates of 50 to 500 liters per second. An additional attracting flow of approximately 500 to 2500 liters per second can be realized for both inflow and outflow. Figuur 2.2: The entire fish pass is designed to be as natural as possible via a natural substrate base (left) and upright built (right). 2.1.1 Underwater connection via the outflow chamber and guide flow opening The FSSG lock is installed underwater within a custom-designed outflow chamber, which also serves as its foundation (Fig. 2.3). This chamber guides fish either ascending to the lock doors or descending to the guide flow opening. To mimic a natural environment, the outflow chamber is filled with base substrate. Figuur 2.3: Inlet of the FSSG. 2.1.2 Upstream connection via the inflow chamber and guide flow opening A watertight inflow chamber is installed upstream of the FSSG lock, its height designed to accommodate the normal fluctuations in surface water levels (Fig. 2.4). This inflow chamber facilitates the targeted movement of fish, guiding those willing to descend to all lock doors and those ascending to the guide flow opening. To mimic a natural environment, the chamber is filled with base substrate. Figuur 2.4: Outlet of the FSSG. 2.1.3 Continuous multi-chamber lock system Due to its design, the function of the multi-chamber lock system (Fig. 2.5) in the FSSG lock cannot be divided into distinct successive phases. Typically, lock systems operate in phases such as swimming in, lifting or lowering, and floating out. In the FSSG lock, these phases can occur simultaneously within the lock chambers, enabling continuous locking without unfavourable dwell times for the fish. The upper and lower water entries into the FSSG lock are through vertically operated, slow-moving lock doors. Figuur 2.5: Valves of the FSSG. Artificial lighting using LED strips is provided. To mimic nature-like conditions inside the FSSG, LED-lighting was operated to approximate day/night conditions with the light being turned off during the night and turned on during the day. The central tube is flood-proof and closed at the top with a translucent dome. Waterproof maintenance accesses are installed at the top of the lock system for cleaning and filling with base substrate. Electrical or hydraulically automated devices for the lock doors are also located here, along with a safety railing to prevent falls. 2.2 Set-up Only one of the three canals built in the system was used in the experimental set-up. Prior to the experiments (Fig. 2.6), the lower and upper tanks were slightly modified by installing a metal plate to direct the flow of the lower valve towards the rank. Additionally, possible escape routes from the test tank were closed with a small mesh sized grid. Potential “shelter” areas under the bottom plates of the valve were also closed off. Figuur 2.6: Front view of the FSSG. Two HDX PIT antennae (30 cm * 40 cm) made of two loops of insulated 4 mm wired welding cable, fixed on a PVC pipe and connected to antenna tuners and permanent OREGON RFID readers, were installed, each on the front of the upper or lower valve. They were both tuned to have a narrow detection range of approximately 15 cm so that fish would be detected when they cross the valve only – and thus enter the system. Preliminary testing of the system was conducted, assuring the efficiency and detection range of the PIT telemetry set-up. 2.3 Fish experiments For the experiments of 15/5/2024 (exp1), 22/5/2024 (exp2) and 29/5/2024 (exp3) 60, 102 and 124 individuals of ide (Leuciscus idus) were used. These fish were bought from fish farm Vandeput in Zonhoven (Belgium) which utilizes fish culture ponds. If possible, fish used for one experiment were re-used for the next to increase the sampling size and assess the effect of experience. In the second experiment 42 fish were re-used while in the last experiment 88 fish were re-used. Valve data was available for the entire duration of the experiments, albeit at different temporal resolutions (see further). It was decided to work with only one species to allow for an acceptable statistical power to draw sound conclusions. Fish were provided with a PIT-tag and the length and weight of each individual was written down. All fish were released together at the start of the experiment (in the morning to early noon) in the lower tank. The lower and upper tank had a water volume of 6.5 m³ (5.0 m length x 1.3 m water level x 1.0 m width) and 17.0 m³ (3.55 m length x 1.05 m width x 4.56 m water level) respectively. The outflow chamber had a water volume of 24.37 m³ (1.2 m width x 4.31 m water level). The inflow chamber was closed of to ensure fish would enter the FSSG. 2.3.1 Environmental conditions Water velocities were measured during preliminary tests under different conditions and ranged between 0.1 m/s to 0.4 m/s (Table 2.1). Environmental measurements were taken at the beginning and at the end of every experiment in the morning to early noon. Water temperature, pH, oxygen percentage and air temperature were on average respectively 17.5 °C, 8.5, 7.0 mg/L and 15.4 °C (Table 2.2). Pit tag data were compressed using the default settings of the function compress of the R package PITCleanr. This data compression involves determining the first and last detection of a series of subsequent detections on a node as well as the number of detections during each slot (from first and last detection). The location where the fish were released (i.e., the lower tank) was designated as the initial node, with the corresponding timestamp marking the start of each fish’s journey. Conversely, the recapture location was identified as the final node, with the corresponding timestamp indicating the end of each fish’s journey. All fish were alive and presumed to still have their tags at the time of release. However, some fish were found dead and/or tagless upon recapture. Due to the low detection rate of the antennas, particularly the upper one, we did not attempt to match unidentified fish with tag IDs from the release data. In a system with higher detectability, it might have been feasible to trace unidentified fish back to known but not-recaptured tag IDs with a reasonable degree of certainty. Unfortunately, this was not the case in our system. For the experiments, for which recapture data was available, fish were only included in the dataset if they were recaptured and identified upon capture. More specifically, detections and observations of fish which were not recaptured, had escaped the system or could not be identified due to tag loss were omitted. For exp1, six fish were found without a tag and 13 fish were not recaptured (six of them because of the absence of a tag). For exp2, three fish were not recaptured. For exp3, one fish was found without a tag and eight fish were not recaptured (one of them because of the absence of a tag). The temporal resolution and range of the valve-opening and pressure data was different between experiments. In order to harmonize the temporal resolution between experiments and to easily link fish data with valve and pressure data, linear interpolation was applied to yield a temporal resolution of one second. A valve was considered open when the opening was larger than 28 cm. For all experiments the valve was considered closed when the opening was less than 3 cm. For every second the time since the last opening was determined. When linking the valve data to the fish data, for passage through the lower and upper valve respectively the first detection and last detection were used. This was done because we were mainly interested in when fish enter (via the lower valve) and leave (via the upper valve) the system. Fish that were used multiple times did not seem to be more or less likely to move up and down the FSSG multiple times within an experiment (Figure 3.2). Detection probability at the upper antenna for exp1, exp2 and exp3 were 6%, 28% and 39%, respectively. 3.2 Entrance efficiency, passage efficiency and overall efficiency Before fish can successfully enter and pass the FSSG they need to be able to find the entrance (i.e., attraction efficiency). Unfortunately, the current experimental set-up does not allow for an assessment of the attraction efficiency as the area in which fish were released was too narrow to be representative for most real-life situations (Triano et al., 2022). Entrance efficiency is defined as the percentage of attracted fish that enter the fishway (Cooke & Hinch, 2013). In this study the entrance efficiency is considered the proportion of tagged fish able to enter the FSSG (i.e., the lower valve) and swim through it. In practice, this is the proportion of released fish detected on either the lower antenna, upper antenna or recaptured in the upper basin. Since all tagged fish are considered to be attracted to the FSSG due to the narrowness of the lower basin and proximity of the entrance of the FSSG, all tagged fish were considered for the entrance efficiency. Entrance efficiency was very different between experiments and was highest for exp1 (0.98) and lowest for exp3 (0.70) (Table 3.3). It should be noted that the calculated metric is most likely an overestimation from the actual entrance efficiency that was obtained in this lab setting. This is because fish in the narrow lower basin had no real other options than move towards the entrance and fish that lingered outside the entrance without entering might also have been detected by the lower antenna. Due to the imperfect detection probability of the lower antenna (exp1: 100%, exp2: 83% and exp3: 83%) fish might have passed through the lower antenna without being detected, resulting in an underestimation of the metric. However, this effect is most likely to be less of an issue compared to the former two. Not only because the detection probability of the lower antenna was relatively high, also because of the combined opportunities of detection at both the lower and upper antennas and the opportunity to recapture fish at the upper basin (i.e., fish that were not detected at the lower antenna but detected at the upper antenna and/or recaptured in the upper basin must have entered at some point and were therefore also labelled as such). Passage efficiency is defined as the percentage of entered fish that successfully pass the FSSG (Cooke & Hinch, 2013). In this study, the passage efficiency is considered the proportion of entered fish that were able to move through the exit of the FSSG. In practice, this is the proportion of fish that are detected on the upper antenna and/or recaptured in the upper basin over the fish that are known to have entered the FSSG (i.e., they were detected on at least one antenna or recaptured in the upper basin). Passage efficiency was more similar between experiments than the entrance efficiency and was highest for exp2 (0.84) and lowest for exp3 (0.68) (Table 3.3). Unfortunately, the pit antenna at the upper valve failed to detect numerous fish (as many fish undetected by the upper antenna were recaptured in the upper basin) and for this reason it was important to also look at the number of fish that were recaptured in the upper basin to determine the passage efficiency. Using both the number of recaptured fish and the detections yielded the highest and most representative passage efficiency as some fish that reached the upper basin might have moved back to the lower basin. Without the pit antenna this would not have been recorded. Nevertheless, because of the very low detectability (exp1: 6%, exp2: 28% and exp3: 39%) the issue remains that fish moving to the upper basin and back to the lower basin or the area between the lower and upper valve, might not always have been detected. In addition, since the number of entered fish is most likely to be an overestimation and given that this is the reference for the estimation of the passage efficiency, the latter might be further underestimated. The passage efficiency calculated here, even the one that combines recapture and detections, is therefore most likely to be an underestimation from the actual passage efficiency that was obtained in this lab setting. In this study, the overall efficiency is considered the proportion of all tagged fish that were able to move through the FSSG. In practice, this is the proportion of fish that are detected on the upper antenna and or recaptured in the upper basin over the total number of tagged fish. As for the entrance efficiency, the overall efficiency was very different between experiments and was highest for exp1 (0.79) and lowest for exp3 (0.47). It should be stressed that in this study all tagged fish were considered attracted fish. If failure to attract would have been accounted for (which was not possible for this study), it is likely that this overall efficiency would be considerably lower. This makes sense as they need to work synchronized. Between experiments there was however a clear difference in the total duration of a cycle and how it was distributed over the different phases (closed, opening, open, and closing). Exp1 to exp3 were more or less similar in the total duration of one cycle (though it seemed to be slightly shorter for exp1) and the distribution among the different phases within a valve. While the lower valve was closed most of the time, the upper valve was open most of the time. For exp1 especially, the time the lower valve was open appeared only slightly more than half of that of exp2 and exp3. Also the time the upper valve was open appeared smaller for exp1, but not to the same level as for the lower valve. Important to note is that the temporal resolution of the valve-opening-measurements of exp1 were more than 10 times coarser than for the other experiments (Table 3.5), which might cause the opening and closing seem to start earlier and later respectively and the duration of the open phase to appear smaller. One might therefore argue that the operational settings of exp1, exp2 and exp3 were most likely to be the same and any difference between them would be the result of other conditions (e.g. learning behaviour of fish or weather conditions and related differences in oxygen concentration and temperature). 4 Discussion For the experiments exp1 to exp3, the cycle duration and phase distribution can be considered the same, though this was not apparent from the data because of the too low temporal resolution of the exp1 valve-opening data. The lower valve was closed most of the time, while the upper valve was open most of the time. Fish generally wait until the valves are completely open before entering and leaving the FSSG, though for the upper valve a relatively large amount of fish also seem to leave the FSSG when the valve is opening or closing. Despite operational settings of the FSSG throughout the experiments of 2024 being fixed, entrance efficiency and passage efficiency varied substantially as they ranged from 0.70 to 0.98, and from 0.68 to 0.84, respectively. It is very difficult to determine the underlying cause behind this difference as these values are not exact (especially the entrance efficiency might have been overestimated due to the experimental design and detection range reaching outside the entrance) and local, potentially interfering, conditions might have been present but were only sporadically measured (e.g. water quality) (Bunt et al., 2012). In addition, though the available results did not indicate any effect, the familiarity with the FSSG of fish that were re-used for the different experiments might have had an effect. The length and weight did however not seem to have any effect on whether fish were able to successfully use the FSSG, nor did it have an effect on the time it took fish to move up the FSSG. Only a limited number of fish went through the FSSG multiple times. Some preliminary tests with other species indicated there was no clear difference between species in the passage succes or passage timing. When assessing fish passage four different aspects should be assessed: attraction efficiency (the proportion of approaching fish that locate the fishway entrance), entrance efficiency (proportion of attracted fish that enter the fishway), passage efficiency (proportion of entered fish that successfully pass the fishway) and overall efficiency (proportion of approach fish that are attracted to, enter, and successfully pass the fishway) (Baker et al., 2019). Regarding the attraction efficiency, it should be noted that fish were forced into the narrow lower basin with no-where else to go than towards the lower valve. It is reasonable to assume that all fish within this lower basin where in the attraction zone of the FSSG and could all be classified as attracted to the FSSG. Whether the provided attraction flow would be strong enough to direct upstream-migrating riverine fish towards the inlet of the FSSG (i.e., What would be the attraction efficiency?) in a real-life situation, could not be assessed under these fixed laboratory settings and would require field tests on sites that resemble the locations the FSSG is intended for or experiments with larger approach zones. The FSSG therefore has the potential to aid fish in their migration, but placement and sound operational settings will most likely be key. Though the relatively low amount of water that passes through the FSSG is beneficial for water managers that want to prevent too much water to flow from one side of a sluice or hydropower installation to the other, it is not ideal to attract fish and make them move through the system. Both the unnatural low amount and the discontinuous, interrupted supply of water via the single inlet (which could be remediated by the use of all three canals in combination with an additional attraction flow (not tested here)) are likely to limit the ability for fish to find the FSSG entrance (i.e., attraction efficiency), enter it (i.e., entrance efficiency) and move successfully through it (i.e., passage efficiency)(Bunt et al., 2012). Assessments of attraction efficiency in real-life situations are strongly advised. Despite its high variability, the entrance efficiency in this study was relatively high (0.70 to 0.98). It is however key to mention here that the calculated entrance efficiency is most likely an overestimation from the actual entrance efficiency that was obtained in this lab setting. Few studies have assessed entrance efficiency before but the few studies available describe mainly lower values. More specifically, Arctic grayling, trout and suckers were found to have an entrance efficiency of 0.44 to 0.79 for a Denil fishway (Triano et al., 2022) while barbel and chub were found to have an entrance efficiency of 0.10 to 0.80 for a vertical slot and multislot fishway (Romão et al., 2021). It should be noted however that not only the design of the fishways in these and our study differed but that also the tested ambient conditions and experimental set-up were distinct. In the first study, 14 field trails were conducted at six Denil fishways with varying slopes in the upper Big Hole River basin (Montana, USA) from June to October. Wild local fish were captured via electrofishing and PIT-tags were inserted. A set-up of four antennas was used to determine attraction, entrance and passage efficiency. The second study, consisted of a lab experiment for which a full-scale model was installed inside a flume with glass walls to be able to visually observe fish movement. Wild-caught fish were used and observers visually determined the moments of entry and passage per fish. Average water velocity within the fishway varied between 0.2 and 0.5 m/s. Despite, the high entrance efficiency established in this study being promising, additional monitoring in more real-life situations is advised as there was no way to quantify the level of overestimation tied up with this metric. Similarly, despite its high variability the passage success was found to be relatively high (0.68-0.84). Unlike the entrance efficiency however, the calculated passage efficiency was most likely an underestimation from the actual passage efficiency that was obtained in this lab setting. Though other fish passage structures are also characterized by a wide range in passage efficiency, on average passage efficiency decreases from nature-like fishways (0.70), to Denil (0.51), vertical-slot (0.45) and pool-and-weir (0.34) fishways (Bunt et al., 2012). The passage efficiency of the FSSG appears to be closest to that of a nature-like fishway which is a very promising outcome. However, the referred to studies of this review were all conducted under natural conditions (Bunt et al., 2012). One lab study on bony herring passing Denil fishways presented a value of 0.88 for a slope of 8 %(Mallen-Cooper & Stuart, 2007), while another lab study reported passage efficiencies on innovative tube fishways between 0.64 and 0.98 (Harris et al., 2020). Though, both field and lab studies are characterized by pronounced variability related to, amongst others, species and fishway type, length and slope (Noonan et al., 2012), lab studies have a tendency to obtain better results than field tests due to the controlled parameters and foreceful nature of the former (Sun et al., 2023). A postive outcome of lab tests should preceed any attempt to implement a system in rivers or canals. However, even after lab tests provide promising results, an assessment under natural conditions is strongly recommended before considering installation on multiple sites. Comparing the overall efficiency, which brings together attraction, entrance and passage efficiency, of this study with the results of other studies is not advised as attraction efficiency could not be assessed. Despite the high efficiencies, entrance time (time from release to entry; most likely an underestimation) and passage time (time from entry to exit) were typically quite high. This was somehow to be expected as approaching fish have to wait for the different valves to open and close. Fish that missed a cycle to hitch along would need to wait for the next. The first 50% of fish that would enter, did so in 100 to 200 minutes while the majority of Arctic grayling, trout and suckers were found to enter a Denil fishway in less than one hour after their release. Passage times are very difficult to compare due to differences in the fishway type, volumetric power dissipation, height drop between pools, slope, obstacle height, pool depth, species and fork length in the fishway (Bravo-Córdoba et al., 2021). Limitations of the study During the first experiment of 2024 it seemed that the temporal resolution of the valve data was too low to capture the moment the valves opened and closed. The last two experiments had sound valve measurement data for the entire duration of the experiment at an adequate temporal resolution. Another important limitation, typical for any laboratory experiment, involves the controlled conditions that not necessarily mimic real-life conditions. Not only will actual river conditions be different from those in the lab, river conditions are also known to vary strongly in time and space. Since in this study laboratory conditions were fixed, the effect environmental conditions might have had, could not be assessed. In addition, the cultured fish themselves, sedated, operated and transported, are unlikely to show the same behaviour (e.g., movement, intent and motivation) as wild fish would under natural conditions (Noonan et al., 2012). Finally, the limitations of the experimental design and pit telemetry set-up also prevented the estimation of attraction efficiency and introduced some important uncertainty tied up with the estimates of the other metrics. 5 Conclusion This study demonstrates that the Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) holds strong potential as an effective fish passage system. The FSSG achieved a relatively high entrance efficiency (0.70–0.98) and passage efficiency (0.68–0.84), performing comparably to nature-like fishways without being significantly influenced by fish length, weight, or species. However, critical limitations inherent to the laboratory setting frame these findings: Efficiency metric uncertainties: Entrance efficiency was likely overestimated due to detection range boundaries extending outside the entrance, whereas passage efficiency was likely underestimated. Uncertain attraction efficiency: Forced entry conditions in the lower basin prevented a true evaluation of attraction flow, which remains a key concern given the system’s low, discontinuous water supply. Delayed passage timing: Entry and transit durations were noticeably high as fish had to wait for valves to open. While these preliminary results confirm the core functionality of the FSSG, lab performance cannot fully predict behavior under dynamic river conditions. Field evaluations in real-world settings are strongly advised to assess attraction efficiency, evaluate operational configurations, and validate passage success in natural fish communities before widespread deployment.
